catalog_quote: This is the most commonly heard pattern. Each word in the utterance, including nonsyllabic words, takes a primary stress. (Stress is nonphonemic and occurs on the penultimate syllable of all words of more than one syllable.) The intonation contour remains level until the penultimate syllable of the final word. Pitch rises on the penultimate syllable, then falls again on the next syllable to the original level unless it is utterance final, in which case it drops yet another level. [p. 120] ... The monosyllabic series 1 pronouns (as well as series 2 pronouns) never stand alone but always follow an open expression or substantive. They are essentially clitics, though they take primary stress in the sentence (see "Intonation" in the Appendix), and so they are written as separate words. [p. 10]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable of every word of two or more syllables; every word in an utterance, including monosyllabic clitic pronouns and particles, receives a primary stress (p. 10: the series 1 and 2 clitic pronouns 'take primary stress in the sentence' and are therefore written as separate words). The basic intonation contour is level with a pitch rise on the penult of the utterance-final word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress placement. Monosyllables (clitic pronouns, particles) also take primary stress. A separate remark (pp. 119-120) says the root-internal sequence a?e is heard as a long vowel a in normal speech (cf. Kalagan a:), but this concerns vowel length, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement made inside the description of the basic utterance intonation pattern ('each word in the utterance.. takes a primary stress'); examples are short sentences with pitch-level numbers, not citation forms. Data from 1956-57 fieldwork in the community of Datu Mama Undas (Notes, p. 107); published 1988 with editorial additions by Ross Errington (SIL, among the Cotabato Manobo since 1976).
new_statements.identity_note: Kerr 1988 describes 'Cotabato Manobo' (= Glottolog cota1241, alias Dulangan Manobo) from 1956-57 fieldwork in the community of Datu Mama Undas, with editorial additions by Ross Errington (SIL, resident among the Cotabato Manobo from 1976); no sub-dialect is named. The Reid 1971 / ABVD list for the same glottocode is labelled 'Kalamansig Cotabato (Paril dialect)'. Kerr notes (p. 120) that Kalagan (a different, Mansakan language) has a: where Manobo has a?e; that is a comparative aside, not a dialect claim.
